questions.q: The first breakdown of food into fine pieces by crushing and chewing with the teeth is called:
questions.a: Mechanical digestion: the teeth break the food into fine pieces by crushing and chewing.

questions.q: A python swallows the animal it preys upon whole, without chewing it. Which statement must still be true before the python's body can use this food?
questions.a: Its complex food components (such as carbohydrate, protein and fat) must still be broken down into simpler forms in its alimentary canal before its body can use them; skipping chewing does not remove this need.
o: Its complex food components must be broken down into simpler forms in its alimentary canal
It needs no digestion at all, because no chewing took place in the mouth
Its body can use the prey as it is, because animal food is already in a simple form
It can use the food only after its teeth have crushed it into fine pieces

questions.q: (a) What is digestion? (b) Name the long tube in which digestion takes place, and say where it begins and where it ends.
s: (a) Digestion: the breaking of complex food components into simpler forms in the body
(b) The alimentary canal, which begins at the mouth and ends at the anus
questions.a: (a) Digestion is the process of breaking complex food components into simpler forms in the body. (b) The alimentary canal; it begins at the mouth and ends at the anus.

questions.q: True or False: Saliva only makes food wet and soft for swallowing; it plays no part in breaking the food down. Give the verdict and a reason.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: besides moistening food, saliva contains a digestive juice that breaks starch into sugar
questions.a: False. Saliva does moisten food and make it easy to swallow, but it also contains a digestive juice that breaks starch into sugar.

questions.q: Answer briefly about keeping the mouth healthy. (a) How many times a day should we brush our teeth and clean our tongue? (b) What should we do after each meal? (c) Name two problems that these habits prevent.
s: (a) Twice a day
(b) Rinse the mouth with water after each meal
(c) Tooth decay and bad smell in the mouth
questions.a: (a) Twice a day. (b) Rinse the mouth with water after each meal. (c) They prevent tooth decay and bad smell in the mouth.

questions.q: Consider the following statements about nutrition in animals. I. Carbohydrate, protein and fat are complex food components that have to be broken down into simpler forms before the body can use them. II. The breaking down of complex food components into simpler forms begins only when the food reaches the stomach. III. The simpler form of food is absorbed by different parts of the alimentary canal and carried to various parts of the body. Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: the breakdown begins in the mouth, where the teeth crush the food and saliva starts breaking starch into sugar, so food is partially digested in the mouth.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Food is partially digested in the mouth. Reason (R): The teeth release a digestive juice that breaks starch into sugar. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false. Food is partially digested in the mouth, but the digestive juice that breaks starch into sugar is in saliva; the teeth only crush and chew the food into fine pieces (mechanical digestion).
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: Sneha takes three test tubes, each with 3 mL of water. Tube X gets small pieces of dry chapati. Tube Y gets chapati that she chewed for 60 seconds. Tube Z gets one spoon of sugar stirred into the water. She adds 3 drops of iodine solution to each tube. (a) Predict the colour in tube X and give the reason. (b) Predict the colour in tube Y and give the reason. (c) Predict whether tube Z turns blue-black and give the reason. (d) Which two tubes, compared, show that chewing with saliva removes the starch from chapati? Tube Z is a control: what possible doubt about tube Y does it rule out?
s: (a) and (b) X blue-black because chapati has starch; Y no or only very light blue-black because saliva broke the starch into sugar
(c) Z does not turn blue-black, because sugar is not starch
(d) X and Y: the same chapati, unchewed and chewed with saliva, so chewing with saliva is the only difference
(d) Z rules out the doubt that sugar itself gives the blue-black colour, so Y's missing colour means starch was turned into sugar
questions.a: (a) Blue-black: chapati contains starch, and iodine gives a blue-black colour with starch. (b) No colour or only a very light blue-black: saliva broke most of the starch into sugar. (c) No blue-black colour: sugar is not starch. (d) X and Y, because they hold the same chapati and differ only in chewing with saliva. Tube Z rules out the doubt that the sugar formed in Y would itself give a blue-black colour; since sugar gives none, the missing colour in Y shows the starch was broken down into sugar.

questions.q: Rohan takes a bite of a dosa. Describe what happens to this bite in his mouth and food pipe by answering: (a) What do his teeth do to it? (b) Give two things that his saliva does to it. (c) What does his tongue do? (d) How does the bite move down the food pipe to the stomach?
s: (a) Teeth crush and chew it into fine pieces (mechanical digestion)
(b) Saliva moistens it, making it soft and easy to swallow
(b) Saliva's digestive juice starts breaking its starch into sugar
(c) Tongue mixes the chewed food with saliva and pushes it into the food pipe
(d) The walls of the food pipe contract and relax in a wave-like motion, pushing it down to the stomach
questions.a: (a) The teeth crush and chew the dosa into fine pieces (mechanical digestion). (b) Saliva moistens it so it is soft and easy to swallow, and its digestive juice starts breaking starch into sugar. (c) The tongue mixes the chewed food with saliva and pushes it into the food pipe (oesophagus). (d) The walls of the food pipe contract and relax in a wave-like motion and push the food down into the stomach.

questions.q: Which organ secretes bile?
questions.a: The liver secretes bile, which is mildly basic.

questions.q: The secretion of the stomach contains digestive juice, acid and mucus. What does the mucus do?
o: It protects the stomach lining from the acid
It breaks down the proteins present in food
It kills many of the harmful bacteria in food
It breaks the fats into tiny droplets
questions.a: The mucus protects the stomach lining from the acid and prevents damage.

questions.q: True or False: Although it is called the small intestine, it is the longest part of the alimentary canal. Give the verdict and a reason.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the small intestine is almost 6 metres long, longer than any other part of the canal
questions.a: True. The small intestine is almost 6 metres long, which makes it the longest part of the alimentary canal.

questions.q: (a) Name the two structures, outside the alimentary canal, that send secretions into the small intestine. (b) Name the secretion that each of them sends.
s: (a) The liver and the pancreas
(b) The liver sends bile and the pancreas sends pancreatic juice
questions.a: (a) The liver and the pancreas. (b) The liver secretes bile and the pancreas secretes pancreatic juice.

questions.q: Rekha's tests show that bile from her liver and pancreatic juice from her pancreas reach her small intestine and work normally. Yet when her meal of dal, rice and ghee leaves the small intestine, its food components have been broken down only part of the way and are not yet in their simplest forms. Which secretion is most likely missing?
questions.a: The digestive juice secreted by the wall of the small intestine is missing: it is the secretion that further breaks down fats, proteins and partially digested carbohydrates into simpler forms after bile and pancreatic juice have acted.
o: The digestive juice secreted by the wall of the small intestine
The digestive juice secreted by the inner lining of the stomach
The mucus secreted by the inner lining of the stomach

questions.q: Match each event in Column I with the part of the alimentary canal where it happens in Column II. Column I: 1. Food is churned and becomes a semi-liquid mass. 2. Digested nutrients pass into the blood. 3. Starch first begins to be broken into sugar. 4. Food is pushed down by wave-like contraction and relaxation from the mouth to the stomach. Column II: A. Stomach B. Small intestine C. Mouth D. Food pipe
questions.a: 1-A, 2-B, 3-C, 4-D: churning into a semi-liquid mass in the stomach, absorption in the small intestine, starch breakdown starting in the mouth, and wave-like pushing in the food pipe.

questions.q: A student says: 'The small intestine absorbs nutrients well only because it is so long.' (a) Is the claim supported by the features your book gives for absorption? Give your verdict. (b) Name the feature of the inner lining of the small intestine that helps absorption, and say how it helps. (c) What is found in the walls of the small intestine, and how does it help the absorbed nutrients reach the body?
questions.a: (a) No. The book gives the length (almost 6 m) only to show that it is the longest part of the canal; the features it gives for absorption are of the lining and the walls, which the claim leaves out. (b) The inner lining is thin and has thousands of finger-like projections that increase the surface area for efficient absorption. (c) Blood vessels lie in the walls, so the digested nutrients pass into the blood, which carries them to different parts of the body.
s: (a) Verdict: not supported; the book's features for absorption are of the lining and walls, not the length
(b) Thin inner lining with thousands of finger-like projections that increase the surface area for absorption
(c) Blood vessels in the walls, so digested nutrients pass into the blood and are carried to all parts of the body

questions.q: In 1822 Alexis St. Martin was shot in the stomach and his wound left a small permanent hole. Through it Dr William Beaumont watched digestion as it happened and studied how different foods were broken down. Suppose, in one such test, he tied three foods to threads, put them into the stomach and pulled them out after an hour. Results: boiled egg (protein) partly broken down; boiled potato (starch) hardly changed; butter (fat) still mostly a lump. (a) Which part of the stomach's secretion explains the result for the egg? (b) Starch digestion begins in the mouth, yet the potato hardly changed in the stomach. In which part of the canal is its starch broken down further, and by which two secretions? (c) Where would the butter mainly be digested, and how would bile help? (d) Beaumont's assistant concludes: 'The stomach is the main place where all foods are digested.' Using all three results, decide whether he is right.
questions.a: (a) The digestive juice of the stomach, helped by the acid, breaks down proteins, so the egg was partly broken down. (b) In the small intestine: pancreatic juice and the digestive juice of the small intestine wall break down carbohydrates such as starch. (c) In the small intestine: bile breaks the fat into tiny droplets, making its digestion easier, and pancreatic juice and the intestinal juice break the fat down. (d) He is wrong: in the stomach only the protein (egg) was partly digested, while the starch and the fat were hardly changed; it is the small intestine, with secretions from its own lining, the liver and the pancreas, that breaks down carbohydrates, proteins and fats.
s: (a) The digestive juice of the stomach, helped by the acid, breaks down proteins
(b) Small intestine: pancreatic juice and the juice of the small intestine wall break down the starch
(c) Small intestine: bile breaks the fat into tiny droplets, and pancreatic juice and intestinal juice break it down
(d) The assistant is wrong: only protein was digested in the stomach; the small intestine breaks down carbohydrates, proteins and fats

questions.q: Compare the stomach and the small intestine on five points: (a) what happens to the form of the food in each, (b) where the secretions acting in each come from, (c) which food components are broken down in each, (d) which of them is the main place where nutrients pass into the blood, and (e) which of the two is the longest part of the canal and how long it is.
s: (a) Stomach churns food into a semi-liquid mass; in the small intestine food is broken into simpler forms ready for absorption
(b) Stomach: its own inner lining; small intestine: its own lining plus the liver and the pancreas
(c) Stomach: proteins; small intestine: carbohydrates, proteins and fats
(d) The small intestine absorbs the digested nutrients into the blood
(e) The small intestine is the longest part of the alimentary canal, almost 6 m long
questions.a: (a) The stomach churns food and turns it into a semi-liquid mass; in the small intestine the food is broken down further into simpler forms. (b) The stomach's secretion comes from its own inner lining; the small intestine receives secretions from its own lining, the liver (bile) and the pancreas (pancreatic juice). (c) The stomach breaks down proteins; in the small intestine carbohydrates, proteins and fats are broken down. (d) The small intestine is where digested nutrients pass into the blood (absorption). (e) The small intestine is almost 6 m long, the longest part of the canal.

questions.q: In which part of the alimentary canal is stool stored until the body is ready to get rid of it?
questions.a: The rectum, the lower part of the large intestine, stores the stool until it is expelled through the anus.

questions.q: After most nutrients have been absorbed, in which order does the undigested food pass through the last parts of the alimentary canal?
o: Large intestine, then rectum, then anus
Rectum, then large intestine, then anus
Large intestine, then anus, then rectum
Rectum, then anus, then large intestine
questions.a: Large intestine, then rectum (its lower part, where stool is stored), then anus (through which it is expelled).

questions.q: (a) Name two kinds of fibre-rich food mentioned in your book. (b) How does eating fibre-rich food help the large intestine?
s: (a) Any two of: fruits, vegetables, whole grains
(b) It helps the large intestine function properly by making the stool easier to pass
questions.a: (a) Any two of fruits, vegetables and whole grains. (b) Fibre-rich food helps the large intestine function properly by making the stool easier to pass.

questions.q: Answer briefly. (a) Name two fermented foods that are good for a healthy digestive system. (b) What do the bacteria living in the large intestine do? (c) Give two eating habits that advances in nutrition science recommend for digestive health.
s: (a) Any two of: curd, buttermilk, shrikhand, kanji, pickles, gundruk, poita bhat
(b) They break down undigested food, especially fibre, and produce essential nutrients
(c) Any two of: eating meals at proper timings, mindful eating, avoiding overeating
questions.a: (a) For example curd and buttermilk (also shrikhand, kanji, pickles, gundruk, poita bhat). (b) They help digestion by breaking down undigested food, especially fibre, and they produce essential nutrients. (c) Eating meals at proper timings, practising mindful eating and avoiding overeating (any two).

questions.q: True or False: Every bacterium in our body is harmful, so a healthy large intestine contains no bacteria. Give the verdict and a reason.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: the large intestine contains bacteria that help digestion by breaking down undigested food, especially fibre, and producing essential nutrients
questions.a: False. The large intestine contains bacteria that help digestion: they break down undigested food, especially fibre, produce essential nutrients and keep the digestive system healthy.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Eating fruits, vegetables and whole grains helps a person pass stool easily. Reason (R): The large intestine absorbs water and some salts from the undigested food. Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. Stool passes easily because these foods are rich in fibre, which helps the large intestine function properly; R only describes how the waste becomes semi-solid.

questions.q: Consider the following statements. I. The Charaka Samhita highlights easily digestible foods and the judicious use of spices such as ginger, black pepper and cumin. II. The large intestine absorbs most of the digested nutrients from the food. III. Eating meals at proper timings and avoiding overeating help keep digestion healthy. Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: most nutrients are digested and absorbed in the small intestine; the large intestine absorbs water and some salts from the undigested food.

questions.q: Megha says: 'Once food leaves the small intestine, digestion and absorption are over, so the large intestine has no real work to do.' A science museum's computer model follows the waste from one meal and reports these readings. Point X (just entering the large intestine): water 360 mL, salts 6 g, fibre 20 g, digested nutrients nearly none. Point Y (halfway along): water 200 mL, salts 5 g, fibre 14 g, many bacteria. Point Z (lowest part, where the waste stays for some hours): water 110 mL, salts 4 g, fibre 10 g, many bacteria. (a) How much water is removed between X and Z? What does this change do to the waste? (b) Between X and Z the waste loses what fraction of its water and what fraction of its salts? Which does the large intestine take out more of? (c) The fibre falls from 20 g to 10 g. What explains this, and what useful substances are produced? (d) Which reading supports part of Megha's claim, and which part? (e) Give your verdict on Megha's claim, using the readings.
questions.a: (a) 360 mL - 110 mL = 250 mL of water is absorbed, so the waste becomes semi-solid stool. (b) Water: 250 of 360 mL, about 69%; salts: 2 of 6 g, about 33%. The large intestine takes out much more water than salts: it absorbs water and some salts. (c) The bacteria living in the large intestine break down undigested food, especially fibre, and produce essential nutrients. (d) Point X, with nearly no digested nutrients, supports the part saying that most nutrients are digested and absorbed in the small intestine. (e) Megha is wrong overall: the readings show the large intestine absorbing 250 mL of water and some salts, its bacteria breaking down half the fibre, and the stool being stored in the rectum (Z) until it is expelled through the anus (egestion).
s: (a) 360 - 110 = 250 mL of water is absorbed, so the waste becomes semi-solid (stool)
(b) Water 250/360, about 69%; salts 2/6, about 33%: much more water than salts is taken out (water and some salts)
(c) The bacteria of the large intestine break down undigested food, especially fibre, and produce essential nutrients
(d) X: digested nutrients nearly none supports that most nutrients are digested and absorbed in the small intestine
(e) Verdict: Megha is wrong; the readings show water and some salts absorbed, fibre broken down by bacteria, and the stool stored at Z (rectum) before egestion

questions.q: Grass-eating animals that bring partially digested food back from the stomach to the mouth for gradual chewing are called:
questions.a: Ruminants. The process of bringing partially digested food back to the mouth for chewing is rumination.

questions.q: Birds do not have teeth. In which part of a bird is its food broken down by the contraction and relaxation of the walls?
questions.a: The gizzard. Its walls contract and relax to break down food, often with the help of grit (small stones) the bird swallows.

questions.q: (a) What is rumination? (b) Name two animals that ruminate.
s: (a) Rumination: partially digested food is brought back from the stomach to the mouth for gradual chewing
(b) Any two of: cow, buffalo, goat
questions.a: (a) Rumination is the process in which partially digested food is brought back from the stomach to the mouth and chewed gradually. (b) Cows and buffaloes (goats are also ruminants).

questions.q: Ramu's family keeps two buffaloes and a flock of hens on their farm near Anand in Gujarat. Every morning the buffaloes graze in a field, quickly biting and swallowing grass. In the afternoon they lie in the shade and keep moving their jaws for a long time, though there is no fodder anywhere near them. Ramu's sister notices that the hens peck up tiny stones from the ground along with the grain they eat. (a) What are the buffaloes chewing in the afternoon? (b) What is this process called? (c) In which chamber of the hen's digestive system are the tiny stones used? (d) How is the grain broken down in that chamber?
s: (a) Partially digested food brought back from the stomach to the mouth
(b) Rumination
(c) The gizzard
(d) The walls of the gizzard contract and relax and, with the grit (small stones), break down the food
questions.a: (a) The grass they swallowed in the morning, now partially digested in the stomach and brought back to the mouth. (b) Rumination; buffaloes are ruminants. (c) The gizzard. (d) The walls of the gizzard contract and relax, and the swallowed grit helps break the grain down.

questions.q: Answer briefly. (a) After a cow has brought its partially digested food back to the mouth and chewed it thoroughly, where does this food go next? (b) Your book says a cow spends about 8 hours a day just chewing its food. What fraction of a 24-hour day is this? (c) Cows ruminate and birds use a gizzard. What does this difference show about the alimentary canal of animals?
s: (a) It passes down the alimentary canal again for further digestion
(b) 8/24 = one-third of the day
(c) Animals show variations in the structure and function of the alimentary canal, to digest different kinds of food in different ways
questions.a: (a) The thoroughly chewed food again passes down the alimentary canal for further digestion. (b) 8 out of 24 hours, which is one-third of the day. (c) Animals show variations in the structure and function of the alimentary canal, adapted to different ways of digesting different kinds of food.

questions.q: Which statement is true of BOTH a cow and a hen?
o: Food is broken down further after being swallowed
Food is chewed again by the teeth after a while
Small stones are swallowed to help grind the food
Food is brought back from the stomach to the mouth
questions.a: Food is broken down further after being swallowed: in the cow, partial digestion takes place in the stomach; in the hen, the gizzard breaks the food down. The other statements fit only one of the two animals.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A buffalo resting in its shed keeps chewing for a long time, while a pigeon swallows small stones along with its grain. Reason (R): Animals show variations in the structure and function of the alimentary canal to adapt to different ways of digesting different kinds of food. Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: the buffalo ruminates and the pigeon breaks its grain in a gizzard with grit, because their alimentary canals are adapted to digesting different kinds of food in different ways.

questions.q: The steps of digestion in a cow are jumbled: 1. Food is brought back to the mouth. 2. Grass is partially chewed. 3. Partial digestion takes place in the stomach. 4. The grass is swallowed into the stomach. 5. Thoroughly chewed food passes down the canal for further digestion. Which is the correct order?
questions.a: 2, 4, 3, 1, 5: the grass is partially chewed, swallowed, partly digested in the stomach, brought back to the mouth for gradual chewing, and then passes down the canal for further digestion.

questions.q: In the lungs, the finest branches of the windpipe end in small balloon-like sacs. These sacs are called:
questions.a: Alveoli: the small balloon-like sacs at the ends of the finest branches in the lungs.

questions.q: What change is seen in freshly prepared lime water when it reacts with carbon dioxide?
o: It stays clear but becomes warm
questions.a: Lime water turns milky (cloudy) when it reacts with carbon dioxide.

questions.q: Match each part in Column I with its role in Column II. Column I: 1. Diaphragm 2. Alveoli 3. Rib cage 4. Hair and mucus in the nasal passages. Column II: A. Protects the lungs B. Trap dust and dirt from the air we breathe in C. Dome-shaped muscle below the lungs that moves down when we breathe in D. Small balloon-like sacs at the ends of the finest branches in the lungs
questions.a: 1-C, 2-D, 3-A, 4-B: the diaphragm is the dome-shaped muscle, the alveoli are the balloon-like sacs, the rib cage protects the lungs, and hair and mucus trap dust.

questions.q: True or False: Even though hair and mucus in the nose filter out much of the dust, some tiny infectious particles can still reach the lungs. Give the verdict and an example from your book.
s: Verdict: True
Example: during the COVID-19 pandemic the SARS-CoV-2 virus affected the respiratory system and caused breathing difficulties and lung problems
questions.a: True. A lot of dust is filtered out, but small infectious particles can get through to the lungs. For example, during the COVID-19 pandemic the SARS-CoV-2 virus affected the respiratory system, causing breathing difficulties and often serious lung problems.

questions.q: (a) Name the dome-shaped muscle that lies below the lungs. (b) In which direction does it move when we breathe in?
s: (a) The diaphragm
(b) It moves downwards during inhalation
questions.a: (a) The diaphragm. (b) It moves downwards when we breathe in, increasing the space inside the chest.

questions.q: Trace the path of the air we breathe in by answering briefly. (a) Through which pair of openings does air enter the body? (b) Through which tube does the air reach the lungs, and into how many branches does it divide? (c) In what do the finest branches inside the lungs end?
s: (a) The nostrils
(b) The windpipe, which forms two branches, one entering each lung
(c) Small balloon-like sacs called alveoli
questions.a: (a) The nostrils (then the nasal passages). (b) The windpipe; it forms two branches, one entering each lung. (c) The finest branches end in small balloon-like sacs called alveoli.

questions.q: Consider the following statements about the human respiratory system. I. During inhalation the space inside the chest becomes smaller, which pulls air in. II. During inhalation the ribs move up and outwards. III. The windpipe forms two branches, one entering each lung. Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II and III only. Statement I is wrong: during inhalation the space inside the chest increases, and that is why air enters the lungs.

questions.q: Kiran makes the breathing model of Activity 9.2: a bottle with its bottom removed, a Y-shaped tube through the lid with two balloons on its forked end, and a thin rubber sheet tied over the open base. (a) What do the two balloons stand for? (b) What does the rubber sheet stand for? (c) What happens to the balloons when Kiran pulls the rubber sheet downwards, and which step of breathing does this show? (d) What happens to the balloons when he releases the sheet upwards, and which step of breathing does this show?
questions.a: (a) The lungs. (b) The diaphragm. (c) The balloons inflate; this shows breathing in (inhalation), when the diaphragm moves down and air enters the lungs. (d) The balloons deflate; this shows breathing out (exhalation), when the diaphragm moves up and air is pushed out of the lungs.
s: (a) The balloons stand for the lungs
(b) The rubber sheet stands for the diaphragm
(c) Pulled down: the balloons inflate, showing inhalation (diaphragm down, air enters the lungs)
(d) Released up: the balloons deflate, showing exhalation (diaphragm up, air pushed out)

questions.q: A nurse wraps a soft tape round Meena's chest and reads it at four moments during deep breathing: P = 70 cm, Q = 74 cm, R = 69 cm, S = 75 cm. At two of these moments Meena had just breathed in fully, and at the other two she had just breathed out fully. (a) At which two moments had she just breathed in? Give the reason from the way her ribs move. (b) At moment S, in which direction had her diaphragm moved, and what had happened to the space inside her chest? (c) Her brother says: 'Air rushes into the lungs first, and that is what pushes the ribs out and the diaphragm down.' Decide whether he is right, and give the correct order of events. (d) Of the two breaths out, P and R, which was the fuller one? Explain using the readings.
questions.a: (a) Q (74 cm) and S (75 cm), the two larger readings: when we breathe in, the ribs move up and outwards and the chest expands. (b) The diaphragm had moved downwards and the space inside the chest had increased, so air entered the lungs. (c) He is wrong: first the ribs move up and outwards and the diaphragm moves down; this increases the space inside the chest, and then air enters the lungs. (d) R (69 cm), because her chest was smaller than at P (70 cm): her ribs had moved further down and inwards and her diaphragm further up, reducing the space more and pushing more air out.
s: (a) Q and S, the larger readings: the ribs move up and outwards and the chest expands when breathing in
(b) At S the diaphragm had moved down and the space inside the chest had increased
(c) Verdict: the brother is wrong
(c) Correct order: ribs up and outwards and diaphragm down, so the chest space increases, then air enters the lungs
(d) R (69 cm), smaller than P (70 cm): ribs further down and inwards, diaphragm further up, more air pushed out

questions.q: Complete the word equation of respiration: Glucose + Oxygen gives ...
questions.a: Glucose + Oxygen gives Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy.

questions.q: (a) Name the system that carries nutrients and oxygen to all parts of the body. (b) Name the three things it includes.
s: (a) The circulatory system
(b) The heart, blood and blood vessels
questions.a: (a) The circulatory system. (b) It includes the heart, blood and blood vessels; the heart pumps blood through the blood vessels.

questions.q: Inhaled air has nearly 21% oxygen and exhaled air has nearly 16-17% oxygen. What does this tell us?
o: Not all of the oxygen we breathe in is used up
All of the oxygen we breathe in is used up
The body adds oxygen to the air before breathing it out
Exhaled air has more oxygen than inhaled air
questions.a: Not all of the oxygen we breathe in is used up: exhaled air still has nearly 16-17% oxygen.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Breathing is a physical process. Reason (R): Respiration uses oxygen to break down glucose and release energy inside the body. Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. Breathing is physical because it is only the movement of air into and out of the lungs; R describes respiration, a different, chemical process.

questions.q: Differentiate between breathing and respiration on three points: (a) what each process does, (b) where each takes place, and (c) whether each is a physical or a chemical process.
s: (a) Breathing brings in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide (inhaling and exhaling air); respiration uses oxygen to break down glucose and release energy
(b) Breathing involves the nose, windpipe and lungs; respiration takes place inside the body using oxygen carried by the blood
(c) Breathing is a physical process; respiration is a chemical process
questions.a: (a) Breathing is inhaling and exhaling air: it brings in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide. Respiration uses oxygen to break down glucose and release energy. (b) Breathing involves the respiratory passages and lungs; respiration takes place inside the body, where oxygen and glucose reach every part. (c) Breathing is a physical process; respiration is a chemical process.

questions.q: A chart of one alveolus shows a blood tube wrapped around it and two arrows. Arrow X points from the air inside the alveolus into the blood. Arrow Y points from the blood into the air inside the alveolus. (a) Which gas does arrow X show? (b) Which gas does arrow Y show, and what happens to it next? (c) Give one feature of the alveoli that lets these gases pass easily.
s: (a) Oxygen, which passes into the blood and is carried to all parts of the body
(b) Carbon dioxide, which is released into the air in the alveoli and then exhaled
(c) The alveoli have thin walls surrounded by fine tubes containing blood
questions.a: (a) Oxygen passes from the alveolus into the blood and is transported to all parts of the body. (b) Carbon dioxide brought by the blood from the body is released into the alveolus and breathed out. (c) The alveoli have thin walls surrounded by fine blood tubes.

questions.q: For a science fair, Farhan builds a working model. A small hand pump pushes red water through a loop of plastic pipes. The loop passes three stations: a bag of balloons labelled 'lungs', a coiled tube labelled 'small intestine', and a block of clay labelled 'brain'. At each station a card says what the red water picks up or drops off. Visitors ask him questions. (a) Which organ and which part of the body do the pump and the red water stand for? (b) What does the red water pick up at the 'lungs' station, and what does it pick up at the 'small intestine' station? (c) At the 'brain' station, write the word equation for what happens to the substances delivered there, so that we can think. (d) Farhan's card on the pipe going from the brain back to the lungs says 'carries nothing'. Decide whether this card is correct and what it should say.
s: (a) The pump stands for the heart and the red water for blood (the pipes are blood vessels)
(b) Oxygen at the lungs; digested nutrients such as glucose at the small intestine
(c) Glucose + Oxygen gives Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy
(d) The card is wrong: the blood carries carbon dioxide (a waste) back to the lungs, where it is released into the alveoli and exhaled
questions.a: (a) The pump is the heart; the red water is blood moving through blood vessels. (b) It picks up oxygen in the lungs and digested nutrients such as glucose in the small intestine. (c) Glucose + Oxygen gives Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy. (d) The card is wrong: the blood returning from the brain carries carbon dioxide, which it releases into the alveoli to be exhaled.

questions.q: Neha takes one deep breath and swims underwater for 30 seconds without breathing. Her arms and legs keep working hard the whole time. Her friend Kabir says: 'For those 30 seconds Neha was neither breathing nor respiring, because no new air was entering her lungs.' (a) Was Neha breathing during the 30 seconds? Use the meaning of breathing. (b) Which process must still have been releasing energy in her arm and leg muscles? Name the two substances that must reach the muscles for it, and say where each comes from. (c) Your book notes that not all the oxygen we breathe in is used up. Use this to explain where the oxygen for (b) could come from, although no new air was entering. (d) Which system carried this oxygen from her lungs to her muscles, and what waste does it carry back to the lungs? (e) Give your verdict on Kabir's claim, using the difference between breathing and respiration.
questions.a: (a) No: breathing is inhaling and exhaling air, and she did neither for those 30 seconds. (b) Respiration, which needs glucose (from digested food absorbed into the blood in the small intestine) and oxygen (from the air in the lungs), both carried by the blood. (c) Her deep breath filled her lungs with air, and not all of its oxygen is used up at once, so oxygen from this air in the alveoli could keep passing into her blood. (d) The circulatory system (heart, blood and blood vessels) carried the oxygen; the blood carries carbon dioxide back to the alveoli. (e) Kabir is only half right: breathing, a physical process, stopped, but respiration, a chemical process inside the body, went on releasing energy for her working muscles.
s: (a) No: breathing is inhaling and exhaling air, and she did neither
(b) Respiration; it needs glucose (from digested food, absorbed in the small intestine) and oxygen (from the lungs), both brought by the blood
(c) Not all the oxygen in the deep breath is used up at once; oxygen from the air in the alveoli keeps passing into the blood
(d) The circulatory system (heart, blood, blood vessels) carries oxygen to the muscles and carbon dioxide back to the alveoli
(e) Verdict: only half right; breathing (physical) stopped but respiration (chemical) continued, releasing energy

questions.q: Most aquatic animals, such as fish, breathe through specialised structures called:
questions.a: Gills, which are richly supplied with blood vessels.

questions.q: A fish, an earthworm, a lizard and an elephant are compared. Which statement about how they take in oxygen is correct, according to your book?
questions.a: Only two of them use lungs; the other two each use a different body part: the lizard and the elephant breathe through lungs, the fish uses gills and the earthworm uses its moist skin.
o: Only two of them use lungs; the other two each use a different body part
All four use lungs, though their lungs are built differently
Only the fish lacks lungs, so the other three all use lungs
Two of them use gills and the other two use lungs

questions.q: Match each body part in Column I with its description in Column II. Column I: 1. Gills 2. Moist skin 3. Lungs 4. Alveoli. Column II: A. Used by most aquatic animals such as fish, and richly supplied with blood vessels B. Used by earthworms for the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide C. Used for breathing by birds, elephants, lizards and snakes D. Small balloon-like sacs in human lungs, surrounded by fine tubes containing blood
questions.a: 1-A, 2-B, 3-C, 4-D: gills in fish, moist skin in earthworms, lungs in birds, elephants, lizards and snakes, and alveoli as the small sacs in human lungs where gases are exchanged with the blood.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A tadpole and the adult frog it grows into do not breathe in the same way. Reason (R): Amphibians use different body parts for breathing at different stages of their life. Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: a frog is an amphibian, so it breathes through gills as a tadpole and uses lungs and skin as an adult.

questions.q: (a) Gills are richly supplied with what? (b) Using your answer to (a), explain between which two things oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged at the gills.
s: (a) Blood vessels
(b) Between the blood in these vessels and the gases dissolved in the water
questions.a: (a) Gills are richly supplied with blood vessels. (b) Oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged across the gills, between the blood in these vessels and the gases dissolved in the water.

questions.q: On a school trip to a lake, Diya writes in her field notebook: 'Fish swim just below the surface. Two cows stand in the shallow water, drinking. A kingfisher (a bird) dives in to catch a fish and flies back to a branch. Earthworms wriggle in the wet mud at the edge.' Back in class she writes: 'All these animals live at the same lake, so they must all take in oxygen in the same way.' (a) How do the fish take in oxygen? (b) Which breathing part do the cows and the kingfisher use, even when they are in the water? (c) Which part does the earthworm use for gas exchange? (d) Using (a) to (c), decide whether Diya's conclusion is correct, and state the idea your book gives instead.
questions.a: (a) Through gills, across which oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged between the blood and the gases dissolved in the water. (b) Lungs: cows and birds breathe through lungs, even when they are in the water. (c) Its moist skin. (d) Diya is wrong: animals at the same lake use gills, lungs or moist skin. The book's idea is that different animals have different breathing mechanisms to suit their unique habitats.
s: (a) Through gills, exchanging gases between the blood and the gases dissolved in the water
(b) Lungs, for both the cows and the kingfisher
(c) The earthworm uses its moist skin
(d) Diya is wrong: the lake's animals use gills, lungs and skin; different animals have different breathing mechanisms to suit their habitats

questions.q: A research team studies three unknown animals. Animals A and B are each kept in a sealed tank that is half water with air above it. After one hour: in A's tank (A stays under water and never comes to the surface) the oxygen dissolved in the water falls from 8 units to 5 units, while the air above stays at 21% oxygen. In B's tank (B comes up to the surface every few minutes) the dissolved oxygen stays at 8 units, while the air above falls from 21% to 19% oxygen. Animal C lives in a sealed box of moist soil; when the soil is allowed to dry, C's skin dries and it soon stops moving, although the air in the box still has 20% oxygen. (a) Which breathing structure does A most likely use? Give the evidence. (b) Which breathing structure does B most likely use? Give the evidence. (c) Through what does C most likely exchange gases? Name the animal from your book that it resembles. (d) Could A be a cow standing in the shallow water of a pond? Decide, using the readings.
s: (a) Gills: only the oxygen dissolved in the water fell, so A takes oxygen from gases dissolved in water
(b) Lungs: only the oxygen in the air fell and B surfaces often, so B breathes air
(c) Its moist skin, like an earthworm: it failed when its skin dried even though oxygen in the air was still there
(d) No: a cow breathes through lungs and would use oxygen from the air, but A used only oxygen dissolved in the water
questions.a: (a) Gills: the oxygen dissolved in the water fell from 8 to 5 units while the air above stayed at 21%, so A takes its oxygen from the gases dissolved in water, as fish do across their gills. (b) Lungs: the dissolved oxygen did not change while the air above fell from 21% to 19%, and B keeps coming up to the surface, so it breathes air. (c) Its moist skin, as an earthworm does: once its skin dried it stopped moving although the box air still had 20% oxygen, so it needs moist skin to take in oxygen. (d) No. A cow breathes through lungs and would take oxygen from the air, but A used only the oxygen dissolved in the water and never came up to the surface.

questions.q: Your book says that different animals have different breathing mechanisms to suit their unique habitats. Which observation is the best example of this idea?
questions.a: A fish in a pond takes oxygen from the water through its gills, while a goat on land breathes through its lungs: two habitats and two different breathing mechanisms. The other observations show animals with the same mechanism, or are about filtering dust.
o: A fish in a pond takes oxygen from the water through its gills, while a goat on land breathes through its lungs
A cow and a goat grazing in the same field both breathe through their lungs
A person breathes through the nose so that hair and mucus trap the dust
A snake and a lizard lying on the same rock both breathe through their lungs

questions.q: Tina says: 'Whether an animal breathes with gills or lungs depends only on whether it lives in water or on land.' Test her claim with three examples from your book and give your verdict.
s: Supporting example: fish living in water use gills, while land animals such as cows, lions and lizards use lungs
Against: the earthworm lives on land but uses its moist skin, not lungs
Against and verdict: the frog changes from gills (tadpole) to lungs and skin (adult), so the claim is too simple; breathing suits the habitat and also the animal and its stage of life
questions.a: Partly true but too simple. Fish in water use gills and many land animals (cows, lions, lizards) use lungs, which supports her. But the earthworm lives on land and uses moist skin, not lungs, and the frog uses gills as a tadpole and lungs and skin as an adult. So breathing mechanisms suit the habitat, but they also differ between animals and with an animal's stage of life.
